title: The Wobbly Signpost Mystery
markdown:
The house had settled into that deep contented hush that only follows a child’s happy sigh. Lily, all warm and tucked in, was lost in dreams, breathing soft as falling feathers. The quiet cue.

Teddy Patch, whose one button eye gleamed with a mischievous glint that always seemed to wink when he was particularly pleased, nudged Hazel with a plush paw.

“She’s asleep,” he whispered, a soft rumble of stuffing, like distant thunder.

Hazel, tail flicking like a question mark trying to decide if it should be an exclamation point, twitched her nose. “The woods are calling, Patch. Something feels wobbly. Like a poorly balanced acorn.”

It was not only Lily’s favourite bedtime-story map, painstakingly drawn with crayon rivers and crayon forests, that was askew. The whole world outside her window had taken a peculiar detour. The old beech woods, usually a comforting maze of familiar paths, seemed to have wandered. The air hummed with a gentle unmistakable confusion, like a poorly tuned fiddle.

“It’s the signpost,” Patch decided, puffing out his chest, though a little stuffing escaped from a seam near his arm, a sure sign of a flutter. “The one by the big oak. It must have gone missing again. That always throws things off kilter.”

Lily always woke with the sun, and she loved to check her map before breakfast. If the signpost was not right, she might get confused, and that was the last thing they wanted.

They slipped out the slightly-ajar back door, a silent pact between stuffed bear and spirited squirrel. Moonlight dappled dew-kissed grass into shimmering silver. In a flash they were at the edge of the allotments, neat rows of sleeping vegetables a stark contrast to the wilder woods. Usually the path was as clear as Lily’s favourite lullaby. Tonight it felt different. Damp earth and pine, overlaid with a faint puzzling sweetness, like forgotten jam tarts.

“Indeed,” squeaked a voice from beneath a rustling pile of fallen leaves. “Point of order. Unauthorised nocturnal perambulation detected. I shall require precise navigational data and a full disclosure of intentions, post-haste.” Mortimer Mole emerged, brushing imaginary dust from an immaculate waistcoat. Tiny spectacles perched precariously.

Hazel sighed, tail giving an exasperated flick. “Mortimer, we’re just going into the woods. Lily’s asleep, and something’s not right.”

“Precisely. And the woods, as per Regulation 7b, subsection iii, of the Woodland Accord, require a properly affixed directional indicator. Without it, chaos is… well, you see the chaos.” He gestured vaguely toward the slightly disorienting path.

Patch shuddered, a ripple through plush. “Chaos. I don’t like chaos. It makes my stuffing itch something fierce. And it feels prickly.”

They pressed on, Mortimer’s pronouncements about adherence to protocol echoing behind them. Familiar trees loomed, shadows twisting like playful ghosts. Forgotten jam tarts on the air. A strange high-pitched hum in their paws. Lily’s map, tucked in Patch’s worn satchel, felt like a jumbled riddle. The river, which should have meandered toward whispering reeds, seemed to flow upstream. The clearing where fairies supposedly held moonlit picnics was now a patch of particularly grumpy-looking brambles, thorns glinting with ill temper.

“This is worse than last time,” Hazel muttered, whiskers quivering. “The blueberries are growing on the oak trees, Patch. And they look awfully sour.”

“And the owl is hooting backwards,” Patch added, button eye wide. “Hoo-oo is definitely not the sound of a normal owl.”

They found it then, near the ancient beech, guardian of the woods. Not the signpost itself, but fragments. A splinter of carved wood, the faint almost apologetic outline of an arrow. Beside it, scattered among fallen leaves, a few vibrant lengths of fabric. Bunting, strung between low branches like quiet colourful flags, fluttered. Festive. Cheerful. Utterly bewilderingly out of place.

“Who would do this?” Patch wondered, voice small.

“Perhaps,” Mortimer piped, having finally caught up, breathing a little more laboured, “it was an act of well-intentioned interference. A rather enthusiastic attempt at beautification, one might surmise.”

And wouldn’t you know it: perched on a high branch, preening with great satisfaction, a robin. Not just any robin. Reginald, known throughout the woodland for his enthusiastic helpfulness, heart as big as his tiny chest.

Reginald chirped, pure unadulterated pride bouncing off silent trees. “I saw the signpost was a bit wobbly. And it looked so lonely, all by itself. So I thought it needs a bit of cheering up. And Lily likes bright colours, doesn’t she? I’ve seen her drawings. So I made it a party.”

Patch and Hazel looked at each other. Lily did like bright colours. The robin, in earnest desire to make things pretty and, he genuinely believed, point the way better, had dismantled the signpost piece by piece and hung it as decoration. He had even found discarded bunting from a forgotten forest fête.

“So you took the signpost?” Patch asked, trying to keep his voice steady.

“Well, yes. And I tidied up the paths a bit too. Made them more direct. More efficient.” A wing toward a very straight, very confusing path that led directly into particularly thorny gorse, less a path than a snagging hazard.

Hazel felt a pang of understanding. Reginald was not trying to cause mischief. He wanted to help. Brighter. Better.

“Reginald,” she said, soft. “You made everything a bit mixed up. The woods need the signpost to be the right way round. It tells everyone where to go so they don’t get lost.”

Reginald drooped. Cheerful chirping subsided into a disappointed warble. “Oh. I didn’t mean to. I just wanted to help Lily’s woods be happy.”

“It’s all right,” Patch said, and this was the important part. He remembered Lily’s face when she read her map, tracing winding paths, eyes full of wonder. A wobble of fear in his stuffing, a desire to turn back. He pushed it down. “We just need to put it back. Can you help us? You know where all the pieces are.”

Reginald’s bright eyes lit up. “Oh, yes. I put them in safe places.”

And so, with Reginald’s enthusiastic and this time much more helpful direction, they gathered the fragments. Mortimer, surprisingly adept with digging paws, helped fit them together, meticulous nature invaluable. Hazel, nimble, innate understanding of how things fit, guided the reassembly, tail flicking with focus. Patch held the largest piece steady, warmth spreading, purpose. He threw himself forward, cushioning its fall with his own plush body, button eye catching moonlight, rough wood pressing against stuffing. A small risk of a tear in the seams. A small price.

Finally the signpost stood tall again, arrow pointing true. The air seemed to exhale. Familiar scent of damp earth and pine settled back, pushing out the puzzling sweetness. Lily’s map, held carefully by Patch, unfurled. The river flowed correctly, a gentle lazy ribbon of silver. The clearing looked welcoming once more.

Patch felt the echo of earlier worry about chaos, drowned by the steady thump of his own brave heart. The woods felt right, and so did he.

Reginald chirped a happy soft farewell, chest no longer puffed with misguided pride. Mortimer, after a final satisfied nod about the restorative power of proper woodland governance, burrowed back underground.

Patch and Hazel stood a moment, moonlight washing over them. The bunting still hung, a colourful gentle reminder of a kind mistake. Hazel tilted her head, listening to the quiet hum of the sleeping forest.

“We did it,” Patch whispered, button eye twinkling.

“We did,” Hazel agreed, a contented sigh, tail a happy relaxed swish.

As the first hint of dawn painted the eastern sky pink and gold, they slipped back into the house. The woods outside felt perfectly, wonderfully right again. Lily would check her map before breakfast. The arrow, for once, would agree with the crayon.
audience: children aged 11-12, amusing night-time woodland adventure for older children
